title: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu
subject: histoire
description: From **March 13** to **May 7, 1954**, a French army besieged in a valley in northern Vietnam surrendered to the Viet Minh. The defeat ended French Indochina.

hero.hook: In a Vietnamese valley, a colonial army learned that the jungle can beat air power.

blocks.text: On **May 7, 1954**, in a valley in northern Vietnam, a European colonial army surrendered. Facing it was the Viet Minh, the Vietnamese independence movement. **Dien Bien Phu** was more than a French disaster. It was the signal that the colonial age was cracking, in the middle of the Cold War.
How did a former history teacher, General **Võ Nguyên Giáp**, defeat a modern army? Through logistics, through patience, and by turning the French certainty of superiority against them.

Since the 1880s, France had ruled Indochina, today Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. In **September 1945**, [[Ho Chi Minh]], founder of the Viet Minh, declared independence. Paris refused. So began the Indochina War: on one side the French expeditionary corps, with tanks and planes; on the other the Viet Minh and its [[guerrilla warfare]] in [[Tonkin]], the north of Vietnam.

blocks.caption: General Võ Nguyên Giáp, the strategist of the Viet Minh

blocks.text: [[General Võ Nguyên Giáp]] never went to a military academy. He said he learned strategy by reading about Napoleon's campaigns in the Hanoi library.

Giáp thought of war in stages: underground work, mobile guerrilla action, then a general offensive. By 1953 he judged his army ready. The French, for their part, were hunting for the ground for one decisive battle.

General **Henri Navarre**, commander of French forces in Indochina, launched **Operation Castor**: build an air and land base at Dien Bien Phu to force the Viet Minh to attack it. In **November 1953**, paratroopers dropped into the basin. The strongpoints were given women's names: Béatrice, Gabrielle, Éliane.

The French calculation was simple. The enemy could never haul heavy artillery through the jungle. Wrong: tens of thousands of porters carried guns and shells on their backs and on reinforced bicycles. The pieces were then hidden on the ridges above the camp.

On **March 13, 1954**, the shelling began. The airstrip was destroyed in the first hours. Colonel **Charles Piroth**, who had promised to silence the enemy guns, killed himself. The siege lasted **55 days**. Under the [[monsoon]], the torrential rains of Asia, the basin turned into a swamp. Every night the Viet Minh trenches crept closer.
On the first day the French fired **6,000** shells. Giáp's guns fired **9,000**, a weight of fire the French staff had thought impossible for a guerrilla army.
The United States refused a massive air intervention. On **May 7**, after hand-to-hand fighting on the Éliane strongpoint, the ceasefire was sounded.

The [[Geneva Accords]] of July 1954 sealed the French departure. Vietnam was split at the **17th parallel**. More than **2,000** French soldiers died and **11,000** were taken prisoner; fewer than **4,000** came home. A few months later, Algeria caught fire. The United States, meanwhile, edged step by step into what would become the [[Vietnam War]].

events.title: Operation Castor
events.detail: The French dug in on the valley floor.

events.title: Geneva Accords
events.detail: The Indochina War ended and Vietnam was divided.

blocks.text: Dien Bien Phu (**March 13 to May 7, 1954**) showed that popular logistics and a patient strategy can defeat a modern colonial army.
